name: Baldwin

origin.raised_by: Found on the farm of John Ball; popularised by Col. Loammi Baldwin

history: A chance seedling from Wilmington, near Boston, first known locally as Woodpecker or Butters; Colonel Loammi Baldwin spread it in the late 18th century and it took his name. It was New England's leading apple for over a century until the severe winter of 1933-34 killed huge numbers of trees.

look.description: Large, roundish fruit flushed and striped bright red over yellow, with prominent pale russet dots.

taste.summary: Very hard, crisp, juicy flesh with a straightforward sweet flavour backed by a mild tartness; growers prize its firm texture more than any complexity. It holds its shape in pies, keeps three months or more and was long the classic New England cider apple.

tree.notes: Large, long-lived tree that is slow to bear and strongly biennial; thin fruit in the 'on' year.

pollination.notes: Triploid with poor pollen: needs two diploid partners flowering in groups 3-5.

climate.best_climates: New England, New York and similar humid continental climates with warm summers and cool autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with severe winters (it was devastated by the 1934 freeze) and hot southern lowlands.

health.other: Bitter pit was once called 'Baldwin spot' after this variety; also biennial bearing and limited winter hardiness.

grow_notes: Plant where winters are not extreme and supply two pollinators. Thin crops hard in heavy years and keep calcium up to reduce bitter pit in storage.

name: Roxbury Russet
history: Arose in Roxbury in the Massachusetts Bay Colony in the mid-1600s and is generally regarded as the oldest named apple variety raised in what is now the United States. It was valued as a winter keeper and cider apple, and Thomas Jefferson grew it at Monticello.

look.description: Dull greenish-yellow apple heavily patched and netted with grey-brown russet, sometimes with a faint bronze cheek.

taste.summary: Dense, firm yellowish flesh, crunchy but not hard, with a sugary, cider-like sweetness, some tartness and a gentle spiciness milder than Golden Russet's; one taster notes a honeyed aftertaste. Improves after a few weeks in store but can shrivel, and the thick, rough skin is slightly bitter. Makes a sweet juice and cider.

tree.notes: Vigorous, long-lived and hardy. Ploidy unconfirmed (one source lists it as triploid); treat it as a poor pollen donor.

pollination.notes: Needs a pollinator; reported as a poor pollinator of other varieties.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, warm-summer climates of New England and the northern US, where it keeps through winter.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid southern lowlands, where flesh texture and keeping suffer.

health.other: Reported to be fairly resistant to scab, fire blight and cedar-apple rust; flesh browns quickly when cut.

grow_notes: A tough, hardy heritage tree for northern orchards. Plant a reliable pollinator, prune lightly to keep fruiting tips, and store the fruit for a month or so before eating or pressing.

name: Newtown Pippin

origin.place: Newtown (now Elmhurst), Queens, Long Island, New York

history: A chance seedling from Newtown on Long Island in the early 1700s, and one of the first American apples exported to Britain; it was later grown in Virginia as Albemarle Pippin and admired by Jefferson. In the 20th century it became a processing and juice apple in California and Oregon.

look.description: Somewhat lopsided, flattened apple, grass-green ripening to yellowish-green, sometimes with a faint pinkish cheek and russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Hard, tight-grained and rather unappetising straight off the tree; after one to two months in store it turns crisp and juicy with a tart-sweet, wine-like and richly aromatic flavour, famously said to carry a hint of pineapple. The cut flesh browns quickly. A versatile apple for eating, pies, juice and cider.

tree.notes: Slow to start cropping and inclined to biennial bearing; needs fertile soil and a long season to finish its fruit.

pollination.notes: Diploid; plant with another variety flowering in groups 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm growing seasons: the Virginia Piedmont, coastal California (Watsonville) and Oregon's Hood River valley.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short summers such as Britain's and New England's leave it small, green and sour.

health.other: Moderate susceptibility to most diseases; prone to storage disorders including bitter pit and internal browning.

grow_notes: Only worth growing where autumns are long and warm. Give rich, well-drained soil and a pollinator, thin heavy crops to limit biennial bearing, and store before eating.

name: Yellow Bellflower

origin.place: Near Crosswicks, Burlington County, New Jersey

history: An 18th-century chance seedling from Burlington County, New Jersey, that spread west with settlers and became a staple of early California orchards; Bellflower in California and Bellflower in Illinois are named after it.

look.description: Large, elongated, tapering fruit with ribs at the eye end, pale lemon-yellow with a soft pinkish cheek on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, fine-grained flesh that is tart and aromatic when picked, mellowing in store into a rich, honeyed, highly flavoured apple; one taster likened it to key lime pie. Used for pies early in the season and for eating later.

tree.notes: Little reliable modern growing data; fruit bruises easily, so handle with care.

pollination.notes: Plant with a compatible pollinator; UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Warm, long-season districts of the eastern US and California, where it was widely planted in the 19th century.
climate.poor_climates: No firm record; probably under-ripens in short, cool seasons.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded; fruit marks and bruises easily.

grow_notes: A heritage choice for warm-summer gardens. Pick carefully to avoid bruising and allow a few weeks in store for the flavour to soften and sweeten.

name: Tolman Sweet

origin.parentage: Unknown; sometimes said to be Sweet Greening x a russet, without firm evidence

history: An old New England sweet apple of uncertain origin, recorded by the early 1820s and grown for well over a century in New York and New England. Its exceptional winter hardiness made it a favoured grafting stock as well as a baking apple.

look.description: Pale butter-yellow, roundish fruit with faint russet dots and a distinctive line running down one side like a seam.

taste.summary: Firm, rather dry flesh with an intensely sweet, low-acid flavour; fairly plain raw but prized for baking, boiling and pickling, which bring out its richness. Also used in sweet ciders.

tree.notes: Hardy, long-lived and productive, though inclined to crop in alternate years. Fruit hangs well on the tree.

pollination.notes: Plant with a pollinator; UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter northern New England, northern New York and similar climates where tenderer varieties fail.
climate.poor_climates: Hot southern regions; not a variety for warm, low-chill areas.

health.other: Disease behaviour poorly documented; fruit bruises readily and needs careful handling.

grow_notes: One of the hardiest old New England apples, good for cold sites. Thin in heavy years to reduce biennial cropping, and handle the fruit gently.
